National Geographic Education: the term comes from the Greek letter delta, a triangle, the shape of many deltas such as the Nile's.
National Geographic Education gives the order Asia, Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica, Europe, Australia. Phys.org's breakdown by size agrees.
National Geographic Education: Asia accounts for almost a third of the world's land (about 44.6 of roughly 149 million km2).
National Geographic Education: in addition to being the smallest continent, Australia is the flattest.

GPS.gov: at least 24 operational satellites, 95% of the time, arranged so users can view at least four from virtually any point on the planet.

GPS.gov: satellites transmit one-way signals giving position and time. NASA: each satellite transmits its position and time. Trimble: receivers work by listening.

NASA: a receiver determines its position by calculating how long the signals took to reach it. NOAA: distance = signal speed x travel time. Trimble: travel time x speed of light.

GPS.gov: the receiver calculates the user's three-dimensional position and time. Guides describe the unknowns as latitude, longitude, altitude and time.
WorldAtlas and dictionary definitions: the antipode is the diametrically opposite point, joined by a line through Earth's center.

WorldAtlas and Brilliant Maps: about 15% of land is antipodal to land. Wikipedia: roughly 15% of land, about 4.4% of Earth's surface.

WorldAtlas: Spain and Portugal's antipodes are in New Zealand. Wikipedia: the antipodes of most of New Zealand's North Island lie in Spain.

NatGeo: oceanic crust 5 to 10 km; continental crust as thick as 70 km. Britannica: crust varies from a few km to 40 km and up to 70 km in some places.
NatGeo: about 2,900 km thick, 84 percent of Earth's volume. Britannica puts the mantle-core boundary at about 2,900 km depth; other references give 84% of volume.
USGS: a handful of mantle rock would be solid rock, but over long periods it flows slowly at about the rate fingernails grow. NatGeo: mostly solid, moves plastically over millions of years.
NatGeo: the core is about 2,900 km below the surface and almost entirely iron and nickel. Britannica: at about 2,900 km the mantle gives way to an iron-nickel outer core.
NatGeo: outer core mostly liquid iron and nickel; the magnetic field is created in the swirling outer core. Convection in the liquid outer core drives the geodynamo.
NatGeo: inner core reaches about 6,000 C, as hot as the Sun's surface, and stays solid under pressure. Discover and IFLScience report the same.
NatGeo: S-waves can't pass through fluids; the shadow where they disappeared showed a liquid layer. IRIS and university texts describe the S-wave shadow zone the same way.
USGS: the only entirely liquid part of Earth's interior is the outer core. NatGeo: the outer core is liquid while the mantle is mostly solid and the inner core solid.
USGS: the lithosphere is broken into moving plates that contain the continents and oceans. NatGeo: the lithosphere, crust and upper mantle, is broken into large rocky plates.
USGS: the lithosphere is broken into moving plates that contain the continents and oceans. NatGeo: the lithosphere, crust and upper mantle, is broken into large rocky plates.
USGS: the rigid lithosphere moves about on the slowly flowing asthenosphere, part of the mantle. NatGeo: due to convection the plates move relative to each other.
USGS: the rigid lithosphere moves about on the slowly flowing asthenosphere, part of the mantle. NatGeo: due to convection the plates move relative to each other.
NatGeo: plates move at rates from two to 15 cm a year. USGS: spreading rates range from under 2.5 cm/yr (Arctic Ridge) to over 15 cm/yr (East Pacific Rise).

USGS: Mid-Atlantic Ridge spreading averages about 2.5 cm/yr; seafloor spreading over the past 100 to 200 million years grew the Atlantic from a tiny inlet. Britannica: Atlantic widening 1 to 10 cm a year.
USGS: divergent boundaries are where new crust is generated as plates pull away; the Mid-Atlantic Ridge is the best known. Britannica describes seafloor spreading along the ridge's rift.
USGS: convergent boundaries are where crust is destroyed as one plate dives under another. NatGeo Ring of Fire: plates overlap at convergent boundaries called subduction zones.
USGS: at transform boundaries plates slide horizontally past each other; the San Andreas fault zone is an example. NatGeo also calls the Pacific-North American border a transform boundary.

USGS FAQ: Pacific Plate moves northwest relative to North American Plate at about 46 mm a year (the rate fingernails grow); LA and SF will one day be adjacent. USGS This Dynamic Earth gives about 5 cm/yr on the San Andreas.
USGS FAQ gives about 46 mm a year, 'the rate your fingernails grow'. USGS Earthquake Facts: San Andreas movement averages 3 to 5 cm a year, about the speed fingernails grow.
Britannica: Pangea first proposed in 1912 by German meteorologist Alfred Wegener. USGS: Wegener introduced continental drift in 1912.
Britannica: Pangea first proposed in 1912 by German meteorologist Alfred Wegener. USGS: Wegener introduced continental drift in 1912.
Britannica: from the Greek pangaia, 'all the Earth'. USGS: Pangaea means 'all lands' in Greek.
Britannica: Pangea was surrounded by a global ocean called Panthalassa. Live Science and Wikipedia agree.
Britannica: began to break apart about 200 million years ago, forming the modern continents. USGS: breakup began about 225 to 200 million years ago.
Britannica: began to break apart about 200 million years ago, forming the modern continents. USGS: breakup began about 225 to 200 million years ago.
NatGeo: the coasts fit like a jigsaw puzzle and Wegener found their rock layers fit too. USGS: the remarkable fit of South America and Africa was part of Wegener's evidence.
NatGeo: the coasts fit like a jigsaw puzzle and Wegener found their rock layers fit too. USGS: the remarkable fit of South America and Africa was part of Wegener's evidence.

NatGeo: seafloor spreading, rifting and subduction were not well established until the 1960s. Maricopa open text: plate tectonics became the accepted theory in the 1960s.

USGS: an earthquake is what happens when two blocks of the earth suddenly slip past one another; the surface is the fault. Britannica and BGS and Lumen geology texts describe a sudden slip along a fault releasing stored strain.

USGS: plate edges are rough and get stuck while the rest keeps moving, until the force overcomes friction. Elastic rebound accounts (Lumen, USGS video): a fault stays stuck until strain overcomes friction, then slips suddenly.
USGS: hypocenter is where the earthquake starts below the surface; epicenter is directly above on the surface. IRIS defines them the same way.

USGS: energy radiates outward as seismic waves like ripples on a pond; earthquakes are recorded by seismographs. Lumen geology: the sudden slip releases energy that propagates outward as seismic waves.
USGS: each whole number is a tenfold increase in measured amplitude and roughly 32 times more energy. PNSN and Minnesota State geology text agree.
Arithmetic from the 32x-per-step rule: 32 x 32 = 1,024, about 1,000. Lumen/PNSN material states a magnitude 7 releases about 1,024 times the energy of a 5.
NatGeo: May 22, 1960, magnitude 9.5, most powerful in recorded history. NOAA SOS: largest recorded by instruments, at least 9.5. USGS event page lists M 9.5.
NatGeo: May 22, 1960, magnitude 9.5, most powerful in recorded history. NOAA SOS: largest recorded by instruments, at least 9.5. USGS event page lists M 9.5.
USGS: magma is lighter than the solid rock around it, so it rises; erupted magma is called lava. NatGeo: ejected magma is called lava.
USGS: the vast majority of earthquakes and volcanic eruptions occur near plate boundaries. NatGeo's Ring of Fire page links most volcanoes to plate boundaries.
NatGeo: along subduction zones, as rock is subducted it melts and becomes magma. USGS: oceanic-continental convergence sustains many active volcanoes such as the Andes and Cascades.
NatGeo: its length is about 40,000 km and it traces boundaries between plates around the Pacific. Britannica: the horseshoe-shaped belt fringing the Pacific is about 40,000 km long.
NatGeo: 75 percent of volcanoes, more than 450, and 90 percent of earthquakes. Britannica: about 75 percent of volcanoes and 90 percent of earthquakes occur in the Ring of Fire.

USGS: the Hawaiian Islands formed more than 3,200 km from the nearest plate boundary, as the Pacific Plate moves over a deep, stationary hotspot. NatGeo and Wikipedia: the Pacific Plate slides over a stationary hotspot, building the islands one after another.

USGS: plate movement carries islands beyond the hotspot and volcanism ceases; islands get older with distance; the Big Island's exposed rocks are under 0.7 million years old. Wikipedia: the Big Island is youngest and ages increase to the northwest.
NOAA NOS: a tsunami is a series of waves caused by earthquakes or undersea volcanic eruptions. NOAA's Tsunami Program describes earthquake-driven seafloor movement generating tsunamis.
USGS: the seafloor is uplifted and down-dropped, pushing the entire water column up and down. NOAA: vertical seafloor movement transfers energy from solid earth to ocean.

NOAA Tsunami Program: tsu means harbor and nami means wave. NOAA NOS: 'tidal wave' is discouraged by oceanographers because tides have little to do with tsunamis. NOAA NCEI also explains tsunami as a Japanese loanword meaning harbor wave.

NOAA NOS: tsunami waves may travel as fast as jet planes over deep waters. NOAA JetStream: in the deep ocean a tsunami can move as fast as a jet plane, over 500 mph.

USGS: in the open ocean the waves are at most several meters high spread over many tens to hundreds of km. NOAA JetStream: in deep water the top rarely rises more than about three feet above the swell.
NOAA NOS: waves slow in shallow water and build to higher heights as depth decreases. USGS: amplitude increases as the tsunami approaches shore.

NOAA SOS: almost 15 hours for the first wave to reach Hawaii; it killed 61 in Hilo. NatGeo: the tsunami raced across the Pacific and killed 61 in Hilo. USGS summary lists 61 deaths in Hawaii.

USGS: about 80 million years ago India was roughly 6,400 km south of Asia, moving north at about 9 m a century. Wikipedia's Indian Plate article gives similar figures.
USGS: the range began to form between 40 and 50 million years ago when India and Eurasia collided. USGS plate-motions page also dates the collision to about 50 million years ago.

USGS: both landmasses have about the same rock density, so neither could be subducted; the pressure was relieved by thrusting skyward. USGS plate-motions page: the plates crumpled along the collision zone.

USGS: the collision has yet to end and the Himalayas continue to rise. Science outlets report India still pushing into Eurasia and the range still rising (rates vary by region, so no figure is stated).

IUGS: summit rocks are Ordovician limestones from a shallow sea containing marine fossils. Britannica: the limestone atop Everest was ocean floor with many marine fossils. Montana State's Everest project agrees.

NatGeo: there are three main types of rocks, sedimentary, igneous and metamorphic. USGS and every intro geology text use the same three classes.

NatGeo rock cycle: igneous rocks form when molten material cools and solidifies. NatGeo magma page: magma that has cooled into a solid is igneous rock.

NatGeo: intrusive rocks cool slowly with large crystals, extrusive rocks cool fast and are fine-grained; granite is igneous; mafic lava cools into basalt. OpenGeology and Lumen: granite is coarse-grained intrusive from slow cooling, basalt fine-grained extrusive from fast-cooling lava.

NatGeo: sedimentary rocks form from pieces of other rock or organic material; the lowest layers become compacted into solid rock. USGS and NPS: sediment buried deeply is compacted and cemented into sedimentary rock.
Britannica: limestone is sedimentary, its grains often fragments of fossil shells from lime-secreting organisms. AMNH and geology.com describe limestone forming from marine shells and skeletons.
NatGeo: metamorphic rocks are changed from their original form by immense heat or pressure. USGS: metamorphism does not melt the rocks.
NatGeo: metamorphic rocks are changed from their original form by immense heat or pressure. USGS: metamorphism does not melt the rocks.
NatGeo metamorphic rocks: limestone changes into marble; granite under heat and pressure becomes gneiss. NatGeo rock cycle and USGS agree.
NatGeo: the rock cycle shows any rock type can become any other. Standard geology texts describe the same cycle between igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rock.
NatGeo rock cycle: weathering breaks down rock, erosion transports fragments, and accumulated sediment becomes sedimentary rock. NatGeo erosion page defines both processes.
NatGeo: weathering breaks down or dissolves rock but does not involve movement; erosion transports material. Science Notes and other references draw the same distinction.
NatGeo: liquid water is the major agent of erosion; wind and glaciers also erode. Science Teaching: most erosion is by liquid water, wind or glacial ice.
NPS geology: the river began carving 5 to 6 million years ago. NPS fly-through: one mile (1.6 km) deep. Live Science and Wikipedia give the same depth and age range.
NPS geology: the river began carving 5 to 6 million years ago. NPS fly-through: one mile (1.6 km) deep. Live Science and Wikipedia give the same depth and age range.

NPS: during floods large rocks and boulders are carried, acting like chisels on the riverbed. EarthDate: floods dragged boulders through the canyon; it is the rocky flood debris, not the water, that does most of the cutting.

NatGeo: erosion bores caves; when water breaks through the back, it forms an arch; continued wave action leaves sea stacks. Wikipedia and an oceanography text: caves become arches, and eroded arches leave stacks.
NatGeo: wind is a powerful agent of erosion that sculpts ventifacts and builds sand dunes. NPS: dunes are mounds of sand created by wind; Lumen: wind erosion and deposition shape deserts.

USGS: Iceland is splitting along the spreading center between the North American and Eurasian Plates. Museum of Science: Iceland's west and east are the trailing edges of those plates. Wikipedia's Geology of Iceland agrees.

USGS: Iceland is splitting along the spreading center between the North American and Eurasian Plates. Museum of Science: Iceland's west and east are the trailing edges of those plates. Wikipedia's Geology of Iceland agrees.

Museum of Science: the ridge is almost all hidden from view; Iceland is where it can be observed. Wikipedia's Mid-Atlantic Ridge and Guide to Iceland call Iceland the place the ridge is visible above sea level.
Þingvellir National Park: the plates break apart and the land between subsides, in a seven-kilometre wide graben. Wikipedia: the park lies in a rift valley marking the plate boundary.
Þingvellir National Park: activity away from boundaries is about two centimetres a year. Dive.is and Guide to Iceland give about 2 cm per year at Silfra/Thingvellir.
Museum of Science: hot spot sources feed Iceland's volcanism along the ridge. Wikipedia: Iceland is volcanic because it lies on the ridge and over a hotspot.

USGS: energy from the sun and the force of gravity drive the continual movement of water. NOAA: the sun drives the water cycle.
USGS describes evaporation, condensation into clouds, precipitation, runoff, streamflow and groundwater. NOAA: water evaporates, condenses into clouds and returns as rain or snow.

USGS: about 90 percent of atmospheric moisture came from oceans, seas, lakes and rivers; the rest from plant transpiration and a little sublimation. Britannica: the principal source of water vapor is the oceans.
Britannica: transpiration is the evaporation of water through minute pores, or stomata, in leaves. USGS describes transpiration as water vapor released from plant leaves.
USGS: once evaporated, a water molecule spends about 10 days in the air. Britannica: residence time of water vapor is about 10 days. A Nature Reviews study gives a mean of 8 to 10 days.
USGS: once evaporated, a water molecule spends about 10 days in the air. Britannica: residence time of water vapor is about 10 days. A Nature Reviews study gives a mean of 8 to 10 days.
NOAA: seas are smaller than oceans, located where land and ocean meet, typically partially enclosed by land. Britannica: seas are smaller, shallower and partially enclosed by land.
NOAA: the Sargasso Sea is the only sea without a land boundary, defined only by ocean currents. Wikipedia and Geography Realm agree it is the only sea without a coast.
NOAA: the average depth of the ocean is about 3,682 m. The Natural History Museum and UNESCO Ocean Literacy give about 3,688 m.
NOAA: Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench is about 10,935 m deep. The Natural History Museum gives 10,935 m from a 2020 survey.

NOAA JetStream: in January 1992 a container ship lost 12 containers; one held 29,000 bathtub toys. Wikipedia and Smithsonian coverage of oceanographer Curtis Ebbesmeyer give 28,800 toys.

NOAA JetStream: ten months later the first toys washed up in Alaska; driven by wind and currents, some drifted into the Atlantic. Wikipedia: the toys began reaching Alaska at the end of 1992 and some later reached the Atlantic.
NOAA: winds drive currents at or near the ocean surface. NOAA Currents tutorial: large-scale surface currents are driven by global wind systems.

NOAA Ocean Exploration: currents transport warm water from the equator toward the poles and cold water back to the tropics. NOAA: currents drive warm water from the Equator and cold water from the poles.
NOAA: the Gulf Stream is a warm current that moves north along Florida, turns east off North Carolina and flows northeast across the Atlantic. Britannica describes the same path.

NOAA: the warm Gulf Stream brings milder winter weather to Bergen, Norway, than to New York. Fjord Norway and Britannica: the region's winters are milder than elsewhere at that latitude thanks to the Gulf Stream.
NOAA: the Gulf Stream establishes the Sargasso Sea's western boundary. Wikipedia: the sea is bounded on the west by the Gulf Stream.

NOAA: thermohaline circulation is driven by density differences due to temperature and salinity; cold, salty water is dense and sinks while warm water stays on the surface. Lumen Earth Science agrees.

NOAA: thermohaline circulation is driven by density differences due to temperature and salinity; cold, salty water is dense and sinks while warm water stays on the surface. Lumen Earth Science agrees.
NOAA: it can take 1,000 years for a parcel of water to complete the global conveyor belt. Other oceanography texts give 1,000 to 2,000 years.
NOAA: waves are most commonly caused by wind; wind-driven waves are created by friction between wind and surface water. NOAA JetStream and Smithsonian Ocean agree.
NOAA: waves transmit energy, not water, and can travel across an entire ocean basin. CK-12 and other physics sources agree waves carry energy rather than matter.
Britannica: erosion creates sea arches, and when they collapse a sea stack is left. Wikipedia (Stack) and Internet Geography describe caves eroding into arches that collapse into stacks.
Britannica: further erosion wears down the sea stack until it disappears. Wikipedia: continued wave attack undercuts stacks until they collapse into stumps.
ABC News: on 3 July 2005 a 50 m limestone pillar of the Twelve Apostles collapsed. Wikipedia: the Apostles are limestone stacks, and a 50 m stack collapsed in July 2005.
NOAA: waves arrive at a slight angle and generate a current parallel to the shoreline. LibreTexts oceanography: waves approaching at an angle create longshore currents.
NOAA: longshore drift transports beach sediment and can cause significant beach erosion. Encyclopedia.com: longshore drift is the transport of sand along a beach by waves breaking at an angle.
Britannica: the Nile, about 6,650 km, is the longest river in the world. National Geographic and Guinness World Records also list the Nile as longest.
Britannica: the Nile flows northward through northeastern Africa to drain into the Mediterranean Sea. National Geographic describes the same course.
Britannica: the Amazon is at least 6,400 km long, and some claim it is longer than the Nile. National Geographic reported a Brazilian study measuring it longer than the Nile.

Britannica: the main problem is the Amazon's start and end points. Scientific American and Explorersweb: there is no consensus on where the rivers start.
USGS: a watershed is an area of land that drains all streams and rainfall to a common outlet; also called a drainage basin. Britannica and NOAA give the same definition.
USGS: you're standing, and everyone is standing, in a watershed. NOAA: no matter where you are, you are in a watershed.
Britannica: the largest drainage system in the world in terms of the volume of its flow and the area of its basin. WWF and Wikipedia agree it has the largest discharge and basin.

Britannica: about one-fifth of all the water that runs off Earth's surface is carried by the Amazon. Amazon Aid and others give about 20 percent of global river discharge (some estimates 15 to 20 percent).
Britannica: a lake is any relatively large body of slowly moving or standing water that occupies an inland basin. National Geographic Education gives a similar definition.
Britannica: the basin-forming mechanism responsible for the most lakes, particularly in the Northern Hemisphere, is glaciation. Wikipedia (Lake) agrees most lakes are glacial in origin.
Britannica: the Wisconsin ice sheet shaped the present Great Lakes during its retreat. Wisconsin Sea Grant: the melting glaciers of the Wisconsin Ice Age left the Great Lakes.
Britannica: Baikal is the deepest continental body of water and the oldest existing freshwater lake, in a rift zone with breaks in Earth's crust. UNESCO: the oldest and deepest lake in the world.
Britannica: about one-fifth of the fresh water on Earth's surface. UNESCO: 20 percent of the world's total unfrozen freshwater reserve.
USGS: salt in the ocean comes from rocks on land; rain breaks down rocks and the ions are carried by streams and rivers to the ocean. NOAA JetStream sea water page agrees.
USGS: in closed basins like the Dead Sea, evaporation leaves minerals behind. Utah Geological Survey: Great Salt Lake has no outlet besides evaporation, so minerals accumulate.
USGS: in closed basins like the Dead Sea, evaporation leaves minerals behind. Utah Geological Survey: Great Salt Lake has no outlet besides evaporation, so minerals accumulate.
Britannica: the Dead Sea receives nearly all its water from the Jordan River. NASA: the Dead Sea has no natural outlet, so water leaves only by evaporation.
Britannica: the Dead Sea receives nearly all its water from the Jordan River. NASA: the Dead Sea has no natural outlet, so water leaves only by evaporation.
NASA: with salt concentration above 30 percent, the lake is nearly ten times saltier than the oceans. BBC Science Focus and others: about 34 percent salinity versus about 3.5 percent for the ocean.
Britannica: the high-density saline water keeps bathers buoyant; the salinity excludes all life except bacteria, and fish carried in die quickly. Wikipedia agrees.
NSIDC: glaciers form when snow remains and accumulates long enough to become ice; new layers bury and compress old ones. Geology.com and LibreTexts describe the same process.
NSIDC: compression forces snow to recrystallize into grains similar in size and shape to sugar grains. AntarcticGlaciers.org: firn has the appearance of wet sugar.
NSIDC: a glacier slowly flows over land; alpine glaciers are frozen rivers of ice flowing under their own weight. Geology.com: under its own weight a glacier flows outward and downward.
NSIDC: Earth has just two ice sheets, one covering most of Greenland and the other spanning Antarctica. Copernicus Climate Change Service also names the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets.
NSIDC: the two ice sheets contain over 68 percent of the fresh water on Earth. USGS: over 68 percent of fresh water is locked in ice and glaciers.
NSIDC: if the entire Antarctic Ice Sheet melted, sea level would rise about 58 m. The Antarctic and Southern Ocean Coalition gives the same figure.
USGS: the oceans hold about 96.5 percent of all Earth's water. USGS Where is Earth's Water: over 96 percent is saline, in the oceans.
USGS: only 2.5 percent of Earth's water is freshwater. Wikipedia (Water resources) gives 2.5 percent as well.

USGS: over 68 percent of freshwater is in ice and glaciers, another 30 percent is in the ground, and only a little more than 1.2 percent is surface water. Wikipedia: 68.9 percent ice, 30.8 percent groundwater.

USGS: over 68 percent of freshwater is in ice and glaciers, another 30 percent is in the ground, and only a little more than 1.2 percent is surface water. Wikipedia: 68.9 percent ice, 30.8 percent groundwater.
Derived from USGS: 96.5 percent ocean; 2.5 percent fresh; a little over 1.2 percent of fresh water at the surface, so 2.5 L x 0.012 = 0.03 L = 30 mL.

USGS: groundwater fills pores and fractures and moves not like rivers below ground but more like water in a sponge. National Geographic Education: aquifers are not underground rivers or lakes.
USGS: usable quantities of groundwater are found only in aquifers, and wells supply water for homes, irrigation and industry. National Geographic Education describes aquifers tapped by wells.
National Geographic: Egypt was known as Kemet, 'black land', a reference to the dark silt of the Nile's flood. Oxford's Griffith Institute and others give the same meaning.

National Geographic: the flood was an annual summertime event; this natural fertilizer made it possible to grow crops supporting a dense population and cities. Wikipedia (Flooding of the Nile) agrees.
National Geographic: until the completion of the Aswan High Dam in 1970, the Nile flooded the valley every year. HISTORY: the dam was completed 21 July 1970 and ended the annual flood.

Britannica Kids: the earliest civilizations developed in river valleys because the land was good for farming, naming Mesopotamia, the Nile, the Indus and the Huang He. Lumen World Civilization lists the same four.
Britannica: Mesopotamia is from a Greek word meaning 'between rivers', the Tigris and Euphrates. World History Encyclopedia and UChicago give the same meaning.

Britannica: artificial irrigation brought water to large stretches of territory through a widely branching network of canals. National Geographic Education: irrigation developed in the Fertile Crescent.

National Geographic Education: named for its rich soils and called the 'cradle of civilization'; irrigation and agriculture developed there because of fertile soil near the rivers. Britannica and UChicago agree.
